topic.title: The Translation Index
topic.shortdesc: The workspace file that records which source files have been translated, into which languages, and from which source version.

body.p: The translation index is a workspace file that records which source files have been translated, where the translated copies live, and which version of each source file the translation was produced from.

section.title: Location and Lifecycle
section.p: By default the index lives at .contentfusion/i18n/translation-index.xml.

The file is created automatically the first time the agent records a translation or copies a non-translatable asset. Commit it to your DITA project repository so translation state travels with branches, merges, and the same access-control model as your content.

section.title: Agent-Maintained, Human-Editable
section.p: Under normal operation you do not need to touch the index yourself. It is maintained by the translation agent.
The agent also keeps entries sorted and writes one entry per line so diffs stay readable and merge conflicts are less likely.

You can always step in. The index is plain XML in your repository, so you can open it in any text editor, review it in pull requests, and edit it directly when that is faster or more precise than re-running the agent. Typical reasons to edit by hand:

ul.li: Force a retranslation: delete the <entry> for a file, or delete the whole index to reset everything (see Redoing Translations).
Fix a bad path: correct a <source href> or <target href> after you moved or renamed files in the repository outside .
Split or reorganize the index: add <include href="..."/> pointers to split a large index into smaller ones. One example is to split by product area: hardware versus software products.
Import existing translations: generate the index from translations created outside (see Importing a Project with Existing Translations).

p.note: If you edit the file by hand, keep the format rules below so the agent can still parse it on the next run.

section.title: File Example
section.p: Here is an example indented to be easier to read.

<translation-index version="1"> <entry lang="de-DE"> <source href="../../en/topics/install.dita" sha="b225ce…"/> <target href="../../de-DE/topics/install.dita" sha="08971e…"/> </entry> <entry lang="fr-FR"> <source href="../../en/topics/install.dita" sha="b225ce…"/> <target href="../../fr-FR/topics/install.dita" sha="500c34…"/> </entry> </translation-index>This example shows one source topic, ../../en/topics/install.dita, translated into two target languages: German (de-DE) and French (fr-FR).

Each <entry> represents one (language, source file) pair. Because both entries point to the same source href, they record two translations of the same English file rather than two different source files.

The identical source sha value in both entries means both translations were produced from the same version of the English topic. The different target href and sha values identify the separate translated files and the exact recorded version of each translation.
See the file format reference for full details.

section.title: Resolving Conflicts
section.p: The format is designed to keep merge conflicts rare (one entry per line, sorted, and splittable across fragments), but conflicts can still arise:

ul.li: The same topic was translated on two different branches. This is uncommon, and is usually avoided by translating a given topic on only one branch. When it does happen, the translated file itself typically conflicts as well; resolve that conflict and retranslate the topic after the merge.
Two branches added different entries at the same place in the index. Keep both entries.

section.p: Translating on a single branch is the simplest way to avoid index conflicts.
